content: The data collection system for violence against women (VAW) includes detailed information about survivors, such as their age, gender identity, education level, employment status, relationship with the perpetrator, and whether they reside with the perpetrator. The minimum dataset also records the type of violence, the time and location of the incident, the mode or form of violence, its frequency, and the time period over which it occurred. Information about the perpetrator, including their age, sex, gender, education level, and employment status, is also collected. Additionally, the services provided to the survivor are documented. For a case to be entered into the database, the only mandatory variables are the survivor's age and gender identity. Initially, the registry used the incident of violence (case report) as the unit of count, and it continues to analyze and report on these data. The reporting form and database also allow for the collection of a unique identifier for each survivor, enabling survivors to be used as the unit of count in records where this information is available. Between 2013 and 2018, 576,360 cases of VAW were registered, and 57% of these included a unique survivor identifier. This unique identifier facilitates additional analyses. For example, among survivors with a recorded unique identifier, 81% had only one contact with a service provider due to VAW. The registry demonstrates the value of using case reports as the unit of count and the importance of collecting unique identifiers to count survivors for specific analyses. This database integrates information from multiple sectors for statistical purposes without functioning as a case management system or requiring an interoperable information management system. In Argentina, data on VAW services and survivors have been used to develop and modify risk assessments and inform policing policies and practices to prevent further violence. The system emphasizes the importance of accessible electronic data for statisticians and public acceptance of data linking and sharing. The guidance outlines three models for collecting and reporting VAW administrative data from different sectors: 1. Sectoral Collection and Sharing: Each sector collects, manages, and analyzes its data, which is then shared with a central reporting institution. Advantages include the ability to count survivors and perpetrators without sharing unique identifiers beyond the regular chain of information sharing. However, this model requires updating sectoral information systems to include relevant VAW variables and ensuring data quality and statistical maturity. Stand-alone datasets by sector may prevent analysis of interactions between survivors and multiple services unless data linking is implemented. 2. Multisectoral Data Collection on a Unified Form: A single, unique VAW administrative data reporting form is compiled, analyzed, and reported by a central institution. This model allows for a VAW-specific register that collects only relevant variables and can incorporate authorized VAW service providers, including civil society organizations (CSOs). However, it may increase the workload for service providers due to double data entry and cannot identify interactions with multiple services unless unique identifiers are shared. 3. Multisectoral and Multi-Institutional Case Management: A unified VAW database documents care, management, and referrals. This model eliminates the burden of double entry if it is the sole record-keeping system. However, it may duplicate other sectoral practices, and sectors like justice, police, and health may be reluctant to participate. Including personally identifiable information requires stringent data security protocols to protect survivors. The Gender-Based Violence Information Management System (GBVIMS) has been used in humanitarian and emergency settings, where dedicated funding supports service delivery and monitoring. In other contexts, pre-existing information systems supported by general budgets are more common. To protect privacy and confidentiality, information-sharing protocols (ISPs) and standard operating procedures (SOPs) are essential. ISPs establish principles for data collection, sharing, management, and reporting, while SOPs provide detailed guidance on data collection and management. These measures ensure compliance with legal and ethical obligations and include provisions for data security, access conditions, and consequences for breaches. Kosovo provides an example of an integrated, unified VAW database established as part of its National Strategy for Protection Against Domestic Violence (2016–2020). The database, housed in the Ministry of Justice, collects information on VAW and institutional responses. It uses the individual (survivor or perpetrator) as the unit of count and allows tracking of cases, referrals, and services provided. Data security and privacy are maintained through role-based access and limited system users. Survivors and perpetrators are identified by national ID or passport numbers, and only the database manager can search by name to ensure data quality. Training is critical for personnel involved in VAW data collection and management. This includes frontline workers, such as nurses, physicians, police officers, judges, and social workers, who interact with survivors and perpetrators. Training focuses on institutional standards for responding to VAW, roles and responsibilities, and non-discriminatory service provision. It also enhances the capacity of service providers to collect and manage VAW administrative data effectively.
